items.headline: What does feeling good today have to do with living longer?
items.body: Almost everything. The habits that help your back this month are the same ones that add healthy years.
items.card: You don't have to trade feeling good now for living long later.

items.headline: Lifespan vs. healthspan
items.body: Lifespan is how long you live. Healthspan is how long you live feeling good and doing things for yourself.
items.caption: Time the average American spends in poor health at the end of life. The largest gap of 183 countries.

source.title: Mayo Clinic study, JAMA Network Open, 2024

items.headline: Get moving again
items.body: Hands-on care to free up stiff joints and calm pain down, so you can get back to work, the gym, and your kids.
items.card: The American College of Physicians lists spinal manipulation among its drug-free first choices for low back pain.

qr.label: How chiropractic care works at Mayfield

items.headline: Is grip strength a vital sign?
items.body: Researchers measured grip strength in about 140,000 adults in 17 countries and followed them for four years.
items.caption: Higher risk of death for every 5 kg drop in grip strength.

items.headline: Training for the next 30 years
items.body: We train how you move: breathing, core control, balance, and strength. Pain relief is step one.
items.card: Rehab isn't only for injuries. It's how you keep getting up off the floor at 80.

items.headline: Looking upstream
items.body: We look for why a problem started: sleep, blood sugar, nutrition, inflammation, stress. Labs when they help.
items.card: A problem and its solution are not in the same neighborhood.

items.headline: Fitness is a number we can move
items.body: In 122,007 treadmill tests, low fitness carried as much risk as smoking or diabetes, or more.
items.caption: Higher risk of death for the least fit compared with the most fit.

source.title: Cleveland Clinic study, JAMA Network Open, 2018

items.headline: Tendon pain that won't quit?
items.body: Plantar fasciitis, tennis elbow, Achilles trouble. Some tendons stall partway through healing and stay sore for months.
items.card: Radial shockwave sends pressure waves into the tendon to nudge that stalled repair back into motion.

items.headline: The easiest longevity habit
items.body: A short walk after meals helps blunt blood sugar spikes. No gym required.
items.card: Start with a 10-minute walk after dinner.

items.headline: Parade season is hard on backs
items.body: Hours on your feet, ladders, coolers, and kids on your shoulders. Stretch before you go and take turns carrying.

items.headline: About half the cells in you aren't human
items.body: Your body is built from roughly 30 trillion human cells. It carries about as many bacteria, mostly in your gut.
items.caption: Estimated bacteria living in and on an average adult.

items.headline: More than half your bones are in your hands and feet
items.body: 54 are in your hands and wrists. 52 are in your feet and ankles.
items.caption: Bones in your hands and feet, out of the adult total.

items.headline: You're taller in the morning
items.body: Your spinal discs soak up fluid while you sleep, then slowly squeeze it out while you're upright all day.
items.card: Most people are about a centimeter taller when they wake up.

items.headline: Your discs eat by moving
items.body: Adult spinal discs have almost no blood supply. Nutrients seep in through the ends of the disc, and movement helps that exchange.
items.card: Sitting still starves your discs. Moving feeds them.

items.headline: Babies have more bones than you
items.body: Many bones fuse as we grow. Five vertebrae fuse into your sacrum, and three to five more form your tailbone.
items.card: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones. An adult has 206.

items.headline: Your heart never takes a day off
items.body: It beats about 100,000 times a day and moves around 2,000 gallons of blood.
items.caption: Heartbeats in an average lifetime.

items.headline: You make a lot of blood
items.body: Red blood cells live about four months, so your bone marrow is always building replacements.
items.caption: New red blood cells your body makes every second.

items.headline: Your brain is expensive to run
items.body: It's about 2% of your body weight but burns around a fifth of your energy at rest.
items.caption: Share of your resting energy used by your brain.

items.headline: 86 billion neurons
items.body: That's roughly how many nerve cells are in your brain, each linked to thousands of others.
items.caption: Neurons in the average adult brain.

source.title: Azevedo et al., Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2009

items.headline: Faster than a race car
items.line: Your fastest nerve signals travel almost 270 mph, brain to toes.

items.headline: A new skeleton every decade
items.body: Bone is living tissue. Your body breaks down old bone and lays down new bone your whole life.
items.card: You replace about 10% of your skeleton each year.

items.headline: The smallest bone you own
items.body: The stapes in your middle ear is about 3 millimeters long. It passes sound vibrations to your inner ear.
items.card: It's smaller than a grain of rice.

items.headline: Your lungs are bigger than they look
items.body: They hold roughly 480 million tiny air sacs where oxygen crosses into your blood.
items.card: Spread flat, those air sacs would cover about 70 square meters, the floor of a small apartment.

items.headline: You give off heat like a light bulb
items.line: A resting adult gives off about 100 watts of heat.

items.headline: Use it or lose it
items.body: After about age 30, adults slowly lose muscle every decade unless they train it.
items.card: Strength training is the best tool we have to slow that loss.

items.headline: Spinal care is ancient
items.body: Around 400 BC, the Hippocratic text On Joints described stretching and pressing on the spine to treat deformities.
items.card: People have been working on spines for more than 2,400 years.

source.title: Historical overview of spinal deformities in ancient Greece, Scoliosis, 2009
